item.title: What the hell is RIGHT with you?
item.description: Most people don’t care about the suffering of animals - or at least not enough to change their behavior or give anything up.
item.content:encoded:
Most people don’t care about the suffering of animals - or at least not enough to change their behavior or give anything up.

Everywhere I go, I see animal products. In the supermarket, people toss dairy, eggs and meat into their carts without any consideration for the animal that produced them - or was them - thinking only about tonight’s dinner. At restaurants, the menus tell the same story. I see customers pick animals from the menu, leaving bits and bones on the plate when they depart.

Indifference everywhere.

But then, on another day, I find myself at an animal rights or vegan event. A place where people gather to learn about helping animals more effectively. I see hundreds of people listening intently, sharing ideas, offering their time, their money, their energy - for beings of another species that they’ll never meet.

I look at these people, and one question pops into my mind:

What the hell is right with you?

Because in a world where most don’t care, you do.

It’s actually a really important question. What did go right with you? How did you become the way you are? Was it somehow your own effort, your choices? Or was it your genes, your parents, your upbringing, the twists and turns of life that shaped you into who you are?

If we knew the answer, maybe we could make everyone care.

I know it doesn’t always feel right. Because the more you care, the more it hurts. But it is right. In fact, I think you’ve been given a gift. The gift of caring. It gives your life purpose - something many people search for until they die. A life with purpose is a more satisfying life.

But even more important, the gift of caring allows you to help - to help all beings, and make this world a kinder place.

So yes, remind yourself often:

Something is profoundly, beautifully right with you.

item.title: Eeew, disgusting! – Should the animal movement aim for the stomach?
item.description: In 1906 American journalist Upton Sinclair published his book The Jungle. With it, he wanted to raise awareness about the terrible working conditions and lives of immigrant workers in the meat industry in his country. Sinclair wrote to create outrage about this situation and thus hopefully improve the lives of these workers.
item.content:encoded:
In 1906 American journalist Upton Sinclair published his book The Jungle. With it, he wanted to raise awareness about the terrible working conditions and lives of immigrant workers in the meat industry in his country. Sinclair wrote to create outrage about this situation and thus hopefully improve the lives of these workers.
The Jungle’s main effect, however, was altogether different from Sinclair’s intentions. Rather than being angry at the working conditions, the general public was shocked and disgusted at the hygiene and health safety issues and hazards that Sinclair had described. This famously led Sinclair to say: “I aimed at their heart, but accidentally hit them in the stomach”.

It’s an interesting statement, and one that to some extent may be applicable to the outreach and campaigns of people concerned about how humans treat farmed animals. The animal protection/vegan movement – in essence a moral movement that wants to reduce suffering and create justice for all sentient beings – also aims at the heart, trying to increase people’s compassion for animals. Usually, what animal protection groups expose with their undercover investigations are horrific living and dying conditions of the animals, with the aim to make people care. Sure enough, these investigations often create a lot of outrage, and undoubtedly help shift attitudes or can lead to legal reforms. I believe they can be very useful.

Still, I wonder if the general public might feel stronger still about unsafe and/or disgusting foods than about “immoral” foods – which means that the political effect of this kind of outrage might be bigger. Here’s an example of quite some time ago now: in 2008, an undercover investigation by Humane World for Animals (back then still called the Humane Society of the United States) showed “workers kicking sick cows and using forklifts to force them to walk”. There was some outrage over these practices, but the real kicker was that the video raised concerns about the safety of meat. Some of this particular product had ended up in school lunches. Consequently, HSUS’s investigation led to the largest meat recall in US history – which, economically, is probably not a good thing for the company in question, or for meat consumption in general. It seemed that in this case, like Upton Sinclair, Humane World had aimed for the heart but kicked in the stomach.

So what if some animal groups, in addition to spreading awareness about cruelty and injustice, would also consciously, intentionally aim for the stomach and try to expose practises that, instead of being (just) immoral or cruel, are (also) unsafe, unhygienic or downright disgusting? (these may look like different aspects, but they all boil down to the idea that these products might be unsafe to eat)

In general, animal-based foods are usually much more able to trigger a reaction of disgust or danger in humans than plant-based foods (that’s presumably evolutionarily adaptive, as the risk of infections from organisms that are closer to us is greater). If you go through lists of the most disgusting foods, you’ll find that the animal foods feature much more prominently than plant-based foods (see for instance this disgusting list). Of note is also that there’s a whole body of literature about disgust (see e.g. this article on animal products and disgust by researcher Jared Piazza). There is probably a relationship between moral and physical disgust, though the direction of the relationship (i.e whether moral beliefs are caused by physical disgust, or the other way round) is debatable.

As food safety requirements for companies increase, hygienic conditions may be less and less of an issue, and certainly in most countries we will no longer come across circumstances as described by Sinclair in his book. But even if they are not present, the production process of some animal foods is so disgusting that showing the bare naked truth could potentially have a big impact. Here, for instance, is a video showing how gummy bears are made (using gelatin, an animal-derived product). Here’s one showing how hot dogs are made. Both videos have over half a million views, indicating also that there might be something viral about disgusting images.

While undercover investigators bravely roam through factory farms, slaughterhouses or meat processing plants, they could seek to collect coverage that creates disgust or reactions around food safety. They could pass on this coverage to other organizations or anonymously to the press if this is not close enough to their own core business. And animal protection organizations could help spread coverage made by other groups or individuals.

Especially in recent years, many omnivores are quick to point out how “unnatural” or “disgusting” they find meat alternatives. At the same time, they’re chewing on pieces of an animal’s body, which usually went through a pretty disgusting process. One of the reasons many or most people are not disgusted by eating the meat of an animal is that the product, both physically and in terms of its image, has been sterilized. Maybe we can help de-sterilize it and help create the physical and moral disgust that decent human beings are bound to feel when they are even thinking about eating the bodies of mistreated creatures.

item.title: What to do about all the vegans falling off the wagon?
item.description: The organization Faunalytics recently came out with a new version of its popular infographic How to Make and Keep a Vegan. The word keep in the title is important: it was the same Faunalytics which in 2014 came out with a study on current and former vegetarians and vegans
item.content:encoded:
The organization Faunalytics recently came out with a new version of its popular infographic How to Make and Keep a Vegan. The word keep in the title is important: it was the same Faunalytics which in 2014 came out with a study on current and former vegetarians and vegans. From that, we learned that 84% of those who try a vegetarian or vegan diet, don’t stick to it and fall off the wagon at some point. Eighty-four percent!

Now I had hoped that more than a decade later, that number would be lower, because of the simple reason that today it should be a lot easier to be vegetarian or vegan. Alas, the number of those who give up is still high. A 2025 poll conducted by YouGov and commissioned by he Vegetarian Resource Group (VRG), among veg*ns (vegetarians & vegans) in the United States shows the following numbers:

  • 2% of the US population is vegan

  • 2% is vegetarian

  • 5% were vegetarian for three or more years, but are today neither vegetarian nor vegan

  • 1.37% were vegan for three or more years, but are today neither vegetarian nor vegan

So the number of people who were at some point vegetarian or vegan (6.37%) is higher than the people who are presently vegetarian or vegan. And this is only counting those who have been vegetarian or vegan for three years or more. No doubt, the number of ex-veg*ns would be higher if we’d count also shorter periods.

What can we learn from this research?

First of all, let’s look at the silver lining. It seems like bad news that so many people give up on being veg*n - and to some extent it is - but it also means that the potential number of veg*ns is a lot higher than it is today. It means that so many more people have considered or may consider going veg*n, and that if we can remove some barriers, there is enormous growth potential for the movement. If all those who started on a veg*n diet, stuck to it, we’d already be a lot closer to critical mass.

Now what are those barriers? According to Faunalytics’ obstacle research, the main barrier back in 2014 was dissatisfaction with the food: “nearly half of lapsed veg*ns experienced cravings, boredom with their veg*n diet, feeling hungry, and other issues related to food dissatisfaction.” Ten years later this may be less of an issue, yet I think we can remain confident that it is still an important part of the reason why people lapse (or don’t start at all). Returning to 2025, in the aforementioned poll, the Vegetarian Resource Group asked people to tick three factors that would cause them not to eat animal products. The second highest ticked item was “alternative products tasted better”. Clearly, we have still a lot of work, not only in the area of food development but also regarding teaching people some new cooking skills. Fortunately there’s an army of social media influencers doing exactly that today.

Can motivation help overcome these barriers?

Obviously, the more motivated someone is, the more adversity they’ll be able to overcome. Now it’s easy to think that increasing people’s ethical (animal-related) motivation is our main task here. I’m not saying it’s not important - but obviously it’s not enough. Still according to the VRG-poll, the most ticked reason that would help people stop using animal products was health: if they knew they’d be healthy without eating those products, they’d more easily give up on them. One can imagine that as long as there are fears about defective health, even quite strong ethical motivation might not be enough (protein concerns are back, in case you haven’t noticed). Moreover, asked about the most important factors in their food decisions, 58% answered taste, 47% cost and 32% personal health - animal welfare was ticked by 7%. This also means, in my view, that while moral motivations may have the most sticking power, it would be misguided to only focus on them, and not on health or environmental motivations: working with these may create a wider funnel for people to get in.

Community

Something else that’s important for people to go and stay vegan is social support. Going veg*n is easier when you do it together with others - and so is staying vegan. Preaching - or catering - to the choir is hence not something redundant. Organizing potlucks among vegans is sometimes frowned upon by ‘real’ activists who are out there in the streets, but if we want a thriving movement, we can’t afford to keep losing people. Being together helps us not just to remain vegan, but also to remain on board as activists.

Pragmatism

The numbers tell us that it is still not easy to go vegan, or to stay vegan. Longtime vegans may disagree and insist that it is easy, but that doesn’t change people’s perception. Rather than doing a lot of wishful thinking and wishful activism, we should be pragmatic. A pragmatic approach to changing people’s eating behavior consists not just of using any argument that might impact our audience, but also of using different asks. We can ask people to reduce, to try Veganuary, to go vegan during weekends… - anything that gets them to try something and cross the threshold, is good. More steps can be taken from there. And for the love of dog, let’s not make veganism harder than it is by insisting on being uber-consistent, and on having to adopt all kinds of political and ideological beliefs as part of the same package.

The wrong question?

Lastly, we may wonder if asking people to go vegan is the wrong question in the first place. Few people go vegan, many more care about animals. Can we ask for different things? Can we give them “permission” (not that it’s ours to give, but okay) to advocate for animals, for the reduction of animal products, even when they are not vegan themselves? I think we should. Can we ask them, perhaps, to donate to organizations that help farmed animals, even though they themselves still consume them or their products? Again, I think we should. Some things are not only easier than going vegan: they might also be more impactful.


Read a lot more about the science of making and keeping vegans.

item.title: To those that can't look away
item.description: Speaking at an animal conference in Oslo, organized by Anima International, I learned that the team had planned a demonstration to introduce newcomers to activism.
item.content:encoded:
Speaking at an animal conference in Oslo, organized by Anima International, I learned that the team had planned a demonstration to introduce newcomers to activism. And so I found myself standing with a placard reading “McDonald’s: Stop fast-growing chickens”, together with a few dozen others, in front of one of the fast-food giant’s restaurants in downtown Oslo. McDonald’s is one of the few chains in Norway that hasn’t yet committed to switch to slower-growing chicken breeds - which would reduce the suffering of the animals to some extent.

We were all dressed in cheap white cleaning suits meant to resemble hazmat gear, while others handed out flyers or spoke with passers-by and journalists. One of us was dressed up as a gigantic chicken. Hundreds of people walked past during the hour we stood there, and if I read their faces correctly, what I saw most often was discomfort. Their jokes, awkward laughter, dismissive comments and averted gazes all seemed to say: I don’t want to think about this. Here and there, someone gave a thumbs-up or asked for more information, but most people just walked on, or went inside for a burger.

The next day at the conference, I attended a small workshop on insect suffering. The speaker, an insect scientist, asked the group about our early experiences with insects. A young woman with a soft, trembling voice recalled finding a butterfly with one broken wing, wondering if she should have gently ended its life. A young man remembered crying for half an hour as a child after seeing a dragonfly crash into an object. Another woman told us she had once held a small funeral for a bee.

It struck me that these childhood experiences were all moments of some personal pain, and that for those who were open to it, there was suffering everywhere in the natural world, even before we knew about slaughterhouses or factory farms.

Perhaps we cried, and our parents saw us cry. And then… how comforting it must have been when they told us - as parents often do, with the best intentions - that we didn’t have to care so much. That the animal probably didn’t feel anything. That it was just nature. Just as, later, we’d hear that animals on farms or in slaughterhouses “don’t really suffer,” or that “it’s over quickly, after a good life.” Or that it’s just the way it is.

The adults caring today - the ones at animal rights conferences - were the children who didn’t buy those stories. The ones who never learned to switch off their empathy. I don’t know if we had a choice, but we took a different path than most. We’ve chosen to look at the suffering and injustice that others ignore. To not tell ourselves stories about it. And to try to do something about it.

That’s hard. Do we get anything in return? I’ve written elsewhere about how a sense of purpose is perhaps its own reward. But sometimes I can’t help fantasizing about some great Hereafter, where everything will be all right, and where, when we arrive, we’ll be welcomed, not just by our own companion animals, but also

By every dog or cat we helped find a home;

By every chicken, pig or cow or fish we didn’t eat;

By every worm we moved from the asphalt back to the earth;

By every animal we ever helped in any way;

And I imagine they might tell us: thank you for not looking away.

But just in case this never happens, I’d like to say it to you, here and now:

Thank you for not looking away.

item.title: Slow Opinion
item.description: A little hesitation can make our world more livable
item.content:encoded:
Looking at the world and everything that seems to go wrong in it, I often catch myself searching for the one thing that would make it better.

Sometimes I think: if only people had more empathy. Or were more rational.

But those qualities are hard to cultivate on command, and we don’t have much control over how empathic or rational we are.

What we might have more control over, though, is the speed at which we form our opinions.

Most people today, both online and offline, jump to opinions about everyone and everything, often without being the least bit informed. This may lead them to be angry at others for no good reason, or to be thoroughly convinced of something without adequate justification.

The opposite of this is an idea that I call slow opinion.

Slow opinion is about taking one’s time to form an opinion about someone or something. Life and people are often too complex to be captured in quick judgments and assessments. So, what if, when reading a news article or social media post that somehow affects us, instead of jumping to conclusions, we’d wonder:

  • what information might I be missing?

  • is this situation perhaps more nuanced than it seems?

  • might some of what I’m reading be biased?

  • could I be biased, or misunderstanding something?

  • is there any alternative explanation that could account for what’s going on?

  • are there any experts - or even just thoughtful, decent people - saying the opposite?

  • am I familiar enough with the counter-arguments?

These questions would, in many cases, lead us to postpone our judgment or opinion. We would want to corroborate or complete the information we have. And in the absence of complete information, we could give the facts and the people the benefit of the doubt, and thus perhaps be more charitable. We could consider all our opinions as preliminary: the opinions that we hold at the moment, but that are subject to change.

We don’t need to have an opinion on everything
Slow opinion also implies that there can be respect for the fact that someone does not right away have an opinion or make a decision, because they lack information, or have not had enough time to think about the matter. Such a suspension of opinion should not be seen as dragging one’s feet, as weakness or a lack of intelligence, but rather as a maturation process.

Downsides of doubting
Still, slow opinion probably shouldn’t be applied in any and all situations. During COVID, for instance, we saw many people “doing their own research”, believing they could achieve better opinions than experts. That’s probably false. Likewise, I can imagine that it served little purpose to be a slow opinionist about slavery in 18th century US. There is the risk of not condemning stuff that one should condemn - or being among the very last to condemn it. And there’s the danger of so-called analysis paralysis: thinking too hard, trying to take too many things into account and hence not coming to a conclusion, or only way too late. It’s a great way to annoy people, and it will block or delay every process.
So in a way, you may want to be a slow opinionist about slow opinion, and doubt the doubt (sorry, couldn’t resist).

In social movements
Any social or political movement - whether focused on justice, environment, identity, or economics - attracts passionate people. Passion is useful, but it often comes with strong convictions and quick judgments. When we finally “wake up” to something we previously overlooked, it’s tempting to think we now see everything clearly, and that there’s little left to question. Yet chances are we surround ourselves with like-minded people and we rarely hear good arguments for another stance - it’s the famous echo chamber.

And within any movement, the strategies, tactics, and communication choices are rarely as obvious as the core values. Here, slow opinion is essential. It helps us stay open to alternative approaches, listen more charitably to each other, and disagree without fracturing the very communities trying to create change. Slow opinion helps us pause and ask: what if other well-intentioned people see something I don’t?

A world of slow opinionsts
Imagine a world in which everyone takes the idea of slow opinion to heart. Where people, when participating in discussions, say “let me think about that, I’ll get back to you”. Where they ask: “do you have a good article about that which I can read?” A world where people are honest with themselves, are open to change their minds, and can disagree in a civilized way.

Taking a little more time - just a breath, a pause, a question - can make our judgments kinder, our conversations calmer, and our world a bit easier to share.

item.title: Why most of my donations go to animals
item.description: The end of the year is the time to give to charity.
item.content:encoded:
The end of the year is the time to give to charity. Since many years, I’ve given away between 10 and 20% of my income. Almost all of that goes to animal causes. Many people might wonder: why focus on animals when there is so much human suffering in the world?

Here are a few reasons why prioritizing animals makes sense to me (largely inspired by Effective Altruism):

The scale and the intensity of animal suffering is immense

Any charity, in one way or another, wants to increase well-being and decrease suffering. When assessing suffering, both the number of beings affected and the intensity of their suffering matter. More beings suffering from x is worse than fewer beings. And excruciating suffering is worse than moderate suffering. It can get more complicated than this, e.g. when we compare a few beings suffering horribly with many more suffering less horribly, but in the case of especially farmed animals, it is safe to say that an incredible amount of beings suffer horribly.

In the case of animals raised or caught for food, we’re talking about billions of animals (trillions if we include invertebrates). Bertrand Russell supposedly said that “the mark of a civilized human is the ability to look at a column of numbers, and weep,” but since many of us connect more to anecdotes and stories than statistics, here’s one case from our sanctuary:

Just last night, an egg-laying hen came in from a factory farm. She has a broken leg and decalcified bones (a condition often caused by the unnaturally high rate of egg production). A spontaneous recovery was impossible, so our vet inserted a titanium pin to set the bone. Had this animal not been rescued, she’d have continued to go through agonizing pain while starving to death. This is an animal that - like many others - doesn’t even show up in the statistics.

All this suffering is very much ignored and underfunded.

Worldwide, all organizations combined dedicated to helping farmed animals have a budget of roughly 260 million dollars. That may sound like a lot until you get some perspective. Just the marketing budget of Restaurant Brands International (the parent company of Burger King) is more than five times higher.

The entire movement for farmed animals employs just a few thousand people. Meanwhile, a single human-focused charity like UNICEF has over seventeen thousand.

So one answer to the question why support farmed animals? is simply: hardly anyone else does.

All this suffering is preventable and solvable

For many problems in the world, we can’t even see a path towards a solution yet. The suffering of farmed animals is a huge challenge, but it can be alleviated or even entirely prevented. You may or may not be a fan of campaigns to improve the well-being of farmed animals by giving them more room, but these are interventions that can make a significant (albeit insufficient) difference for millions or billions of beings. Even making their death less painful is worth pursuing. But - at least in theory - we can see a path towards abolishing this suffering altogether. If we can somehow replace animal products with alternatives, we can end 99% of all human-caused animal suffering in the world.

You can’t rationally discount animal suffering

Of course there are many worthwhile causes beyond farmed animals. But the arguments above should at least convince any rational person that non-humans, too, are entirely worthy of our donations. The only reason to ignore them altogether would be to claim that they don’t morally count—or count only for very little. I don’t see any valid grounds for that. Pain is pain, suffering is suffering, no matter who experiences it.

Yes, there may be cases where humans can suffer more intensely than non-humans. We can take that into account, and I don’t object if people place somewhat higher moral weight on human beings. But this is still no reason to discount animal suffering entirely - to the point that we might prefer donating to help a museum acquire more artworks rather than to an NGO trying to stop, for example, the unanesthetized castration of millions of piglets.

Where to give?

Assuming you want to spend part of this year’s donations on animals, here are some quick pointers.

As Effective Altruists know, some organizations deliver a lot more suffering-alleviating bang for the buck than others. It should not be taboo to compare various organizations’ impact: when you buy a phone, you’ll look for a model with good price/quality. Why would you not do that in the case of something much more important: reducing suffering and saving lives?

It would take too much space to look at organizations in detail, but fortunately we don’t have to do that here. There are organizations evaluating other organizations, to see how good of a job they do. In the farmed animal sphere, you can look at the recommendations of Animal Charity Evaluators, Farmkind, the Effective Altruism Animal Welfare Fund, Founder’s Pledge or Giving What We can. Note that their recommendations are very valuable but they’re not everything. There might be great organizations that didn’t get the chance to get evaluated, or weren’t selected for some reason that might not be relevant to you.

These meta-organizations don’t just recommend: you can also give through them. You can either earmark your money for one or a few specific organizations, or put it in the meta-organization’s fund, from which it will be distributed to their recommended charities.

Don’t beat yourself up if you don’t manage to give exclusively to organizations that have been identified as effective. I have a rational donation budget and an emotional one. The first one is the biggest, the second one is for impulse donations or causes that I’m particularly partial to (oh my god, dogs!)

Also, don’t be afraid to donate to (animal or other) causes that many people might find weird - which in itself is a reason why they’re probably underfunded. Examples are the Shrimp Welfare Project, Wild Animal Initiative, or the Insect Welfare Research Society. No matter how exotic a cause might sound, all animals - particularly big groups of them - need at least a few people and organizations looking into them.

Some other organizations I’m personally affiliated with and am therefore partial to:

Feathery Forest, our own sanctuary. We’re definitely not the most effective organization in the world in terms of animals we rescue, but we do a lot with little. If you want to donate, click here.

Proveg International: an organization I co-founded. We do, I think, great work in the field of food system change in 17 countries.

OPIS: organization for the prevention of intense suffering by humans and non-humans.

And you can of course support this very newsletter if you find it valuable.

Since I have many readers from Belgium and the Netherlands: two meta-charities that will regrant the money you give them to effective causes and organizations, are Effectief Geven (BE) and Doneer Effectief (NL)

Talk about your giving

You might not be in a position to donate today, and that is of course totally fine. But don’t think that too fast - you may be richer than you realize. And if you are well-off, then please, dig a little deeper in your wallet. Less suffering and increased well-being is the best thing your money could ever buy.

As a final point: when you give, let it be known. We all post plenty of silly or trivial things on social media, yet many of us hesitate to share the things that actually matter. But people take their cues for what counts as good behavior from those around them. When they regularly see friends and peers donating, they become more inclined to donate themselves. Normalizing generosity helps create more of it.

I hope the above makes clear that giving to animals - and particularly farmed animals - is a worthwhile cause, because the scale and intensity of their suffering is immense, because few people do it, and because we can make tremendous progress in this field.

Thanks for whatever you do, and happy holidays!

item.title: Sources of solace: ten things I do to stay (sort of) sane in this world
item.description: I started working in the animal movement around 1996.
item.content:encoded:
I started working in the animal movement around 1996. Thirty years later, I’m still active. That’s probably not as common as one might wish. One of the questions I get asked most often is how I manage to stay engaged and remain hopeful.

We obviously do not have complete control over how happy, optimistic, or energetic we are. Much of that is determined by our genes and our upbringing. I, for instance, am by nature not the most optimistic or cheerful person; I’m prone to mood swings, some anxiety and obsessive thinking. Still, I do believe there are things we can do that help. Here’s what I rely on to keep going.

1. Seeking the company of like-minded people
This world contains more suffering and injustice than most people would ever want to know about, but one of the greatest sources of solace is realizing that one is not alone in trying to make things better - and that many beautiful things are happening. My partner is a very dedicated animal activist, and many of my friends are too, or are at least deeply caring people. If you have few or no like-minded people around you, I recommend that, if possible, you join local events or attend a conference, so you can recharge your batteries and make deep connections with others.

2. Focusing on the good and the beautiful
If you’re not around like-minded people and hardly ever encounter activists, you can still get inspired by what you read and watch online (see my post about elevation - what you feel when you see others being good). Even looking at something terrible, you can direct your own attention to the positive. When I see a horrible video, for instance, I think about the commitment of the people who made it, and the wonders of technology that allow us to spread this content far and wide.

3. Being grateful for caring
Gratitude can increase one’s well-being. No matter the challenges, everyone can find things to be grateful for. We can be grateful for having a sense of purpose, or for being sensitive to suffering - because without that, we wouldn’t have the same motivation to make things better.

4. Knowing that impatience is not an option
We’re trying to change the deep-seated beliefs and behaviors of billions of people. This is possibly the biggest endeavour a group of people has ever taken on. That’s not going to be a quick process. This is not a marathon; it’s an ultramarathon.

5. Seeing people as buckets
I see people as buckets that have to be filled with compassion, awareness, facts, experiences… all the things they need in order to change. When their bucket is full, they change. We can suspect but can’t really know, at any point, how full the bucket is. We can only add the drops that we are adding, and know that other people will add other drops, in many ways.

6. Seeing people as victims
While altruism and collaboration are certainly useful in nature, I believe the process of natural selection has made sure we are often fretful, anxious and distrustful. Our own nature doesn’t always work with us. If you can see everyone - including the meanest people - as victims of natural selection, it becomes easier to tolerate how they behave. And you can always think: but for luck, that person could have been me.

7. Believing that I chose to be here
If I were living on a distant planet where all is well and everyone was happy, I believe that, upon learning about what happens on Earth, I’d want to go there. So I like to think that, living this life on this planet, I am where I choose and need to be, however unpleasant it is at times. Read Refusing nirvana.

8. Avoiding toxic behavior
I don’t believe much in bad people, but some individuals can definitely behave in nasty ways. Sadly, my worst confrontations have been with other vegans, criticizing me for not being radical enough, not being a real vegan, or whatever. I do welcome constructive criticism and challenges to my views, but when people are consistently nasty, dishonest or untrustworthy, I will often block them on my social media. Life is better without their input.

9. Sometimes: witnessing suffering
I focus on the positive, and I don’t recommend that people who are already aware watch horrible footage on a daily basis. Still, every now and then, I will watch some infuriating video of animal abuse - glimpsing through my fingers, my other hand ready to click the horror away. I do this because I know that, sometimes, when done in moderation, it can deepen my motivation.

10. Allowing myself to be highly imperfect
I had a serious burnout ten years ago, and that didn’t help animals. Guilt, self-reproach and the feeling that I should always do more are not reliable fuels for long-term change. Sometimes the most ethical thing to do is to rest, to enjoy beauty, to live a reasonably good life. Exhausted people don’t change the world. (See Are animal people too good for their own good?)

None of the above guarantees optimism or peace of mind. Nor does it make the suffering disappear. But holding these things in mind makes it possible for me to keep showing up.

I wish you a lot of energy and hope.

item.title: On respect for vegans and meat-eaters
item.description: Says the meat-eater: “I respect the fact that you don’t eat meat, but I expect you to respect my choice as well.”
item.content:encoded:
Says the meat-eater: “I respect the fact that you don’t eat meat, but I expect you to respect my choice as well.”

A brief word about that respect.

We should always respect each other as human beings, and respect each other’s freedom. No one can or should force anyone else to do anything.

At the same time, we can distinguish between respect for people and how we view certain choices these people make. I can respect someone who eats meat, while at the same time having reservations about the choices he or she makes.

To think that respect for eating meat and respect for eating plant-based are on the same level is, I think, misguided.

When a meat-eater says that they respect my choice to be vegan, I always think: Really? Isn’t that the bare minimum?

I then try to put myself in the meat-eater’s shoes. Maybe they think the vegetarian/vegan is being dramatic, difficult, following a trend, trying to be special… and that those things don’t necessarily call for respect.

But for the vegan, it’s about something else. It’s about boycotting or reducing suffering and exploitation. And for that, he or she is willing to forgo certain pleasures and tasty things. He or she says: I may find this tasty, but I’m not going to eat it. An effort is being made to help bring about change. I think that does deserve a certain amount of respect.

Conversely, the meat-eater asks for respect for… what, exactly? I honestly don’t find it easy to respect the fact that someone consumes and enjoys something carelessly, at the expense of the suffering and death of others. Nor do I have much respect for gratuitous opinions that are poorly grounded.

Still, I continue to respect the person. This will undoubtedly sound paternalistic or condescending to meat-eaters (so be it), but I understand that change is not equally easy for everyone. I try to remember that I needed time too. I respect that people get stuck in patterns of thinking and habits. That they sometimes do things to please others. That they worry about their health, about farmers, about a society that is often very critical. I see that people sometimes feel their identity is under threat, and that traditions - even if they mean little compared to suffering and death - are not unimportant or worthless.

In short, I do my best to stay open, to listen, and to understand.

That, for me, is what respect means in this context.

And hopefully, from there, we can move a small step forward.

item.title: Brigitte Bardot, antispeciesism, and the temptation of moral simplicity
item.description: Among vegans and animal advocates - most of whom are quite progressive - many reactions to the death of French movie star Brigitte Bardot have been decidedly negative. Even if she helped animals, she was a racist and a bigot.
item.content:encoded:
Among vegans and animal advocates - most of whom are quite progressive - many reactions to the death of French movie star Brigitte Bardot have been decidedly negative. Even if she helped animals, she was a racist and a bigot. Therefore she should be neither celebrated nor remembered. End of story.

It’s an understandable response. And it would be easy for me to condemn her unequivocally. Doing so, I’d win approval in the circles where I feel most at home. It would demonstrate that I am on the right side (meaning the left side). Yet I think it would also risk betraying the animals. So if you’re open for some additional nuance, read on (if you think nuance is a bad thing, you may want to read my slow opinion article first).

All of this is my preliminary opinion, based on what I’ve read. It’s possible that I’m overlooking points that would change my view. Anyway, no matter how many caveats I put here, I realize this text might be misinterpreted anyway. So be it.

A moral asymmetry
Antispeciesism is grounded in more general principles of justice, equity, and the rejection of arbitrary exclusion. Racism and homophobia violate those principles. From that perspective, condemnation of Bardot can feel almost obligatory.

I want to suggest that reducing people like Bardot to being racists - full stop - may be morally too simple, strategically counterproductive and, paradoxically, revealing of a deep asymmetry that antispeciesism is meant to challenge.

“Nothing excuses racism, and nothing can make up for it” sounds strong, uncompromising, and morally clear. But taken literally, it is also misleading, whether we apply it to Bardot or to anyone else. If nothing can ever make up for racism, then moral accounting becomes into a binary: once someone has crossed that line, everything else becomes morally irrelevant. Their actions, sacrifices, achievements, even the lives they may have saved, do not count compared to the hateful words they spoke.

Yet even the most committed antiracist or antispeciesist does not apply this logic consistently. We coexist daily with people who participate in, benefit from, and defend a system that inflicts immense suffering on animals. We continue to love them, work with them, organize with them, vote with them. I hope we don’t reduce them to animal abusers, even though part of us may think that is what they are.

I understand, of course, that we’re talking about different norms, and that in our society it’s hard to measure our treatment of humans and animals by exactly the same yardstick. But when someone like Bardot is reduced entirely to her worst statements about people, we should at least pause and ask why this reduction suddenly feels so natural, and why we may even feel pushed to respond this way.

Part of the answer, I think, lies in the moral asymmetry we still carry - sometimes unconsciously - even as antispeciesists. Of course it is possible to do so much harm in one domain that it eclipses all the good one does in another. But when we dismiss a lifetime of animal advocacy because of the words a person said (words which, it is true, may have real-life consequences), animal lives are once again being treated as morally secondary, as if their protection does not weigh heavily enough to complicate the verdict. It’s moral accounting where the animals don’t show up on the balance sheet.

Left behind
Bardot didn’t just make harmful comments, but also supported far-right politicians. To understand better why she did that, we need to realize what she was confronting, at a time when most of us animal advocates were not yet active: a machine turning billions of sentient beings into food, entertainment, clothes, or research subjects. Bardot was furious about it (even though, as a vegetarian, she still participated in some of it).

The point is, her hateful remarks do not seem to be simple expressions of xenophobia or bigotry. Many of them appear to be rooted in a broader misanthropy, because of what humans do to animals. When she described some people on Réunion Island as savages, it was apparently because they used puppies as live bait for fishing. When she spoke about “barbaric Muslims” invading France, it was because she was furious about the ritual slaughter of sheep by members of the Muslim community.

But Bardot - a combative, uncompromising and at times reckless personality - did not only attack immigrants or minorities; she also fiercely condemned French culture itself for its treatment of animals. She lashed out at any practices she saw as cruel, backward, or barbaric.

If you take animal suffering seriously and see the moral catastrophe that is happening every day, it’s not hard to imagine how rage can at times turn into something ugly when it finds no constructive outlet. Especially when the political camp - the left - that claims compassion as a core value, leaves animal suffering structurally under-addressed, one might feel drawn to allies that do take animals seriously, even if they bring toxic ideas. Bardot herself said bluntly that had the communists taken animals seriously, she would have allied with them instead of with far-right parties.

Some will object that condemning Bardot is not only a matter of principle, but also of strategy and pragmatism: drawing a hard line is necessary to keep animal advocacy respectable and to win (or at least not alienate) the left.

I understand this concern. But it rests on the assumption that the left, as it actually exists, has been a reliable or sufficient vehicle for the cause of reducing animal suffering. Evidently it has not. Despite its language of justice and compassion, the left has largely tolerated, normalized, or sidelined the mass abuse of animals. Recognizing this is not a blanket endorsement of right-wing politics, nor a call to compromise on anti-racism or other core commitments. But if this is the political reality, animal advocates among the right are a strategic necessity (we can criticize them for other views they hold).

Rejecting moral simplicity
We should be able to hold two truths at once: Brigitte Bardot’s racist and homophobic statements were indefensible, and her work for animals was extraordinarily significant. Rejecting moral simplicity does not weaken our ethics but strengthens them. Just like Bardot could do a lot better than reducing a group of people to their most horrible behavior towards animals, all of us can do better than reducing an entire person’s life to her racist or bigoted rhetoric.

Bardot’s life forces us to ask difficult questions about moral purity, strategic alliances, and the place animals still occupy - even within movements built to defend them. If antispeciesism is to be more than a slogan, it must be able to look at such cases without flinching, and without reaching too quickly for comforting certainties.

item.title: When all the pent-up anger and sadness comes out
item.description: Me vs. the hunters
item.content:encoded:
Planet Earth can be a pretty nasty place. There are many things Homo sapiens does that revolt me, but usually I somehow manage to keep myself together.

Not so when I run into a group of hunters on a peaceful nature walk.

This time, I really tried. I made an effort to hold myself back. I passed about five men with guns just as they were getting out of their cars, wearing their fluorescent vests. One of them greeted me politely. I managed to simply ignore him - which is a bit of an achievement.

I walked into the forest and saw that they followed the same path, behind me. Not much later I heard a gunshot, and saw three or four roe deer fleeing among the trees.

At that moment, I unleash my demons. I turn around, walk back, and confront two of the hunters, walking through the woods with rifles at the ready.

“You having fun?” I say in a loud voice.

“Excuse me?”

“Are you enjoying killing animals?”

A deep sigh. “Sir, you are on private property. You have to go back to the road.”

“Is this your land?” I ask.

“No, but we have hunting rights here. You need to leave.”

“Then call the police, because I’m not leaving,” I say angrily, not exactly sure what I want to do. I’m now just two feet away from him.

“I should call the police? Sir, you are the one on private property.”

“I know. Call the police or the owner.” I’m shouting now.

“Sir, you have no reason to come after me like this.”

“I do have a reason!”

“Really?”

“I’m defending the innocent animals you’re trying to kill.”

Another deep, frustrated sigh. “And tonight on your plate,” the hunter says, “it’ll be cauliflower, I guess?”

I’d heard this before, during an earlier confrontation with hunters. Maybe it’s something they teach in hunting school: if you run into some half-crazed anti-hunting type, ask them what they’re having for dinner. Gotcha!

“I haven’t eaten meat for thirty years,” I say.

“Looks like it,” the hunter replies. “Lack of development.” The irony of that remark seems to escape him entirely.

“Come on, let’s get out of here,” says his hunting buddy, just as frustrated as he is.

They disappear into the forest. I continue on my way.

When I hear another gunshot, I can’t help myself. I cup my hands around my mouth and shout as loud as I can: “Cowaaaaaaaaards!!”

The word echoes over the hills.

I’m told I usually look like a calm and composed person, so those of you who ever heard me speak or read my writings might be surprised that I’ve got this rage in me. Actually, when it comes out, it surprises me too.

But then again, it shouldn’t. It’s the pent-up anger, frustration and sadness about what’s happening to the animals, that I carry inside me quietly, day in, day out, for many years now. Rage at suffering, injustice, indifference. Those hunters got a full load.

I’m quite ambivalent about raging at them like that. On the one hand, it does feel good to do something. I believe that if everyone who meets hunters, challenges them, this may help to de-normalize hunting and maybe make their little outing just a little bit less pleasant. And potentially, it’s good for me to vent, just now and then. It certainly feels good. Liberating even. I feel no fear, not even much adrenaline. Just… righteous indignation.

On the other hand, everything I talk about to vegans and animal activists - tolerance, kindness, empathy, trying to take the other’s perspective - I threw it all out the window with this action, and probably didn’t achieve anything.

I know I can have a coffee with a hunter and have a decent discussion. We’ll agree on some things. For instance on the fact that wild caught-meat is better than factory-farmed meat. If I’m in a charitable mood, I might even admit that now and then, a good hunter may reduce suffering, by countering overpopulation and making sure the animals don’t have to starve to death. I can ask a hunter, from a place of genuine interest, why they do what they do. I could listen and nod, and really do my best to try to understand what pleasure their hobby brings them.

But not during the act itself. Not in the moment when animals are being terrorized, running for their lives. Not when right in front of me, someone aims to hurt and kill an innocent deer. In that case, apparently, I don’t have myself under control.

Maybe the next time in encounter a hunter in the woods, I’ll make an effort to keep my calm and approach him like a Zenmaster, or at least like the psychology-literate person I aspire to be.

Not making any promises, though.

item.title: When doing something good makes other people hate you
item.description: Reactance, do-gooder derogation, and our one universal fear
item.content:encoded:
I’ve seen vegans (and vegan arguments) attacked, vilified, and ridiculed for decades. But is it just me, or has it gotten noticeably worse in the last few years? And why is it that doing something meant to reduce harm can turn you into a target for a significant part of the population?

The immediate cause for writing this piece was a barrage of comments I received on a few Facebook posts from omnivores pushing back against an animal-friendly message. One could call these people trolls, but I’ll try to be charitable here.

I heard the familiar arguments. About health. About the Amazon rainforest being destroyed for my tofu. About plants feeling pain. None of that was new. Two other reactions weren’t new either, but I was struck by how often they came up - seemingly even more than they used to.

The first was: “You vegans think you’re morally superior.”

The second was: “Stop telling us what to do.”

These are old and tired arguments (or rather, emotional responses) but they are very revealing - especially when seen in the context of both the current zeitgeist and some features of human psychology.

To explain what I mean, let me take you back almost two decades.

Our one universal fear

It’s 2006. Together with a good friend and thousands of others, I’m standing in a huge hangar somewhere in the north of London. On the podium in front of us - shouting, bouncing, waving, fist-bumping - is the self-help guru of gurus: Tony Robbins.

“What are we all afraid of?” Tony asks.

We’ve heard it a few times already, so we can all shout along:

“That we’re not ENOUGH!”

“And if we’re not enough…?” Tony shouts back.

“We won’t be LOVED!”

I can still see and hear it. Ten thousand people chanting it, recognising it, fearing it. Tony claimed this fear was universal - present across cultures, classes, and circumstances. Rich or poor, he said, admired or ignored, successful or struggling: at some level, we all fear not being enough, and therefore not being loved.

However high your disdain for self-help gurus may be, at the very least in my own experience, Tony is right. Some part of my mind tells me this (literally) dozens of times a day, in one form or another: you’re not enough. You should do more. Be better. Work harder. Others are doing better than you. You’re an impostor. And so on, ad nauseam.

I’m guessing I’m not the only one, and Tony is correct that more or less everyone has this fear. And nobody enjoys being reminded of it.

Moral threat

I think you can see where I’m going with this. One important reason why people attack vegans (and other people perceived as “do-gooders”) is not primarily disagreement about facts or arguments, but a sense of moral threat. When someone does something that is widely seen as good, it can make others feel worse about themselves, whether they want that to happen or not.

This phenomenon even has a name in psychology: do-gooder derogation. We tend to dislike, dismiss, or ridicule those whose behaviour implicitly suggests that we could - and perhaps should - do better.

Seen in this light, accusations of “moral superiority” make sense. Often, no explicit claim of superiority is being made at all. The mere act of opting out of a harmful norm can be experienced as a silent reproach.

And yes - this is uncomfortable to admit, but important nevertheless - part of the reason many of us are vegan (or do good) is probably that it does make us feel better about ourselves. That doesn’t invalidate the choice. Almost all moral behaviour has a self-affirming component. Wanting to see yourself as someone who tries to do less harm is not a character flaw, but probably part and parcel of how motivation works.

The problem arises when that self-affirmation in one person triggers self-doubt in another - a dynamic which is likely intensified today. We live in a time of uncertainty, status anxiety, and perceived loss - economic, cultural, and symbolic. There is widespread resentment toward “educated city people,” experts, and so-called elites. Veganism, fairly or not, often gets lumped into that category: another lifestyle choice associated with moralising, privilege, and telling others how to live.

From that perspective, “stop telling us what to do” is less a response to an actual command than an expression of reactance: the instinctive pushback we feel when our freedom or moral self-image seems threatened. None of this means that the hostility toward any sort of do-gooder is justified. But it does make it more intelligible.

Being charitable

I am not suggesting that we respond to hostile comments by telling people they’re insecure, afraid, or morally fragile. That would only make things worse. Nor am I suggesting we abandon moral clarity or stop advocating for animals. What I am suggesting is that we take seriously the idea that many aggressive reactions are rooted in fear - specifically, the fear of not being enough, and not being loved.

So what to do with this? As I sometimes say: the true test of compassion lies not in being kind to the weakest, but in being charitable toward those we find most irritating, unreasonable, or hostile. This is much easier said than done. In online discussions, it is incredibly tempting to go into attack mode. Many commenters write in all caps, make spelling mistakes, repeat the same bad arguments. It is so easy to mock, belittle, or score points.

But every time we make someone feel smaller, dumber, or morally inferior, we strengthen the very reactance that keeps them stuck. And this ultimately keeps animals suffering.

Our ego might enjoy the clash. Our sense of righteousness might even be gratified. But if the goal is fewer animals harmed, more minds opened, and more hearts shifted, then understanding this psychological dynamic is not a luxury, but part of the work.

(PS: you are enough)

item.title: All of This Is Allowed
item.description: Walking through the forest near my home, I can often smell the pig farm barely a stone’s throw away.
item.content:encoded:
Walking through the forest near my home, I can often smell the pig farm barely a stone’s throw away. The environmental damage caused by that pork factory is serious enough in itself, but what occupies my mind most when I pass by are the animals who live there and never see daylight. I occasionally hear the pigs squeal, but I have never actually seen one. I simply know they are there - until they are sent to the slaughterhouse and turned into pork chops for humans. Other animals will take their place. An unending cycle.

A bit further on, I come across two small dogs who are locked up in a small kennel. Their owners have a large garden, but perhaps they don’t feel like fencing it off. Or maybe they don’t want to clean dog poop from the lawn. I’ve rung their doorbell a couple of times, but never found anyone home. I’ve asked the police, who went to check things out, but told me they couldn’t see anything illegal. Holding dogs like that is just as legal as cramming pigs together in a dark shed.

From the garden with the dogs, I walk a few hundred meters further and pass a house. Through the window, I can see a birdcage with a lone bird inside. That cage would be the size of a room for a human - a room in which we’d have to spend our entire lives. Now imagine having wings, which allow you to move in three dimensions and, if you wish, to fly for hours on end. I suspect the elderly lady who “owns” the bird has no idea how limited - almost nonexistent - the freedom of movement of her little companion really is.

On the same walk, I may encounter other instances of animal suffering: hunters shooting rabbits and deer. Anglers who, in their own Zen-like way, drive a hook through a fish’s mouth. A rat who’s been poisoned. Herd animals who are alone. Ducks without water.

All of this is allowed. All of this is legal.

Every single day, I am amazed by this: that we as a species invent the most incredible things, create beautiful art in countless forms, slowly unravel the mysteries of the universe with telescopes we send millions of kilometers into space… and at the same time still imprison, abuse, exploit and kill billions of non-humans at will.

This situation becomes stranger still when you realize that a majority of people, across cultures, seems to genuinely care about animals. Just one survey from my country shows that 84% of respondents believe animals should not have the legal status of object, and they can suffer in the same way humans do.

A survey is, of course, only a survey, but this one and many others leave little doubt that at least in theory, across many countries, there is broad concern for animals and large public support for greater animal welfare.

Why, then, one might ask, is change happening so slowly? Why are we still barbarians when it comes to our treatment of the non-humans with whom we share the planet?

Many answers can be given to that question. We treat animals shamefully because we can. We do it because we want cheap meat. Because we are used to it and it’s been like this for a long time. Because change is difficult. Because of social pressure. Because vested interests resist…

But above all, animal suffering persists because most people somehow manage to look away from it. The irony is that they do so precisely because confronting animal suffering is often painful. But such wilfull ignorance, of course, solves nothing. One of the first things we must do if we want to rid the world of animal suffering - any suffering - is to be willing to see it.

It is a question that has haunted me for decades now - and that I will keep exploring, in articles here, and I think for the rest of my life:

How to make people see?

item.title: "Don't tell me what to eat!"
item.description: Why Food Freedom Fighters are mistaken
item.content:encoded:
Vegan arguments are usually pretty solid. Yet vegan messaging fails more often than it succeeds.

There are many reasons why this is so. The one I will address here is that people often resist being persuaded - especially when they feel someone is trying to change them. This resistance to persuasion stems, among other things, from a desire to see ourselves as free individuals who make our own choices.

Some people are much more sensitive to threats to their freedom than others. Moral psychologist Jonathan Haidt, in his Moral Foundations Theory, describes “liberty versus oppression” as one of the key moral dimensions people vary on. For many, this liberty sensitivity functions almost like an emotional alarm system: the moment they sense someone is trying to control them, they push back - often before they’ve even considered the substance of the message.

This is especially true for libertarians, for whom personal autonomy is often the central moral lens through which almost every political and ethical issue is judged. This includes food. Here, I’ll refer to people who attach very high importance to autonomy in matters of diet as food freedom fighters.

When freedom trumps everything else

Many limits on our freedom are uncontroversial. We accept (at least in theory) that we don’t have the freedom to rob others of their freedom - or their lives, bodily integrity, or property. Other freedoms are contested, like the right to bear arms in the United States. And what we consider acceptable changes over time, along with our moral norms. Practices that were once taken for granted can later become subject to scrutiny, regulation, or outright bans. The freedom to smoke wherever you like, for instance, is a thing of the past in most countries.

When it comes to food - and the consequences of our dietary choices - freedom still seems to trump almost any other argument. No matter the scale at which we exploit animals, the intensity of their suffering, or the damage done to the environment and public health, meat, dairy, and eggs can be produced legally, and people are free to buy them. That is the reality today. And until there is broader consensus that many of these practices are wrong or at least problematic, we have little choice but to accept this appeal to freedom of choice. Whenever we suggest otherwise, we’re told - politely or not - to stop telling people what to do.

Now when our messaging and attempts to raise awareness collide with pro-freedom arguments, what can we do? Below I discuss two options.

A rational argument: are omnivores really free to choose what they eat?

Many food freedom fighters won’t be open to rational argument. But those who are willing to reflect honestly may concede that freedom of choice is, to a significant extent, an illusion. I’m not referring here to the philosophical debate about free will, but simply to the forces that shape our food choices.

Of course the average supermarket shopper still decides whether tonight’s meal will feature sausage or pork chops, with fries or mashed potatoes. But how free is that choice really? How much of it is shaped by culture and habit - by what our parents ate - rather than by deliberate reflection?

And how much is steered by food companies and supermarkets that actively develop and promote products that are the most profitable? Through discounts, advertising, product placement, store layout, in-store sampling, scent marketing, and more, retailers and restaurant chains continuously push consumers in specific directions. Cooking shows feature famous chefs using sponsored ingredients. Here’s one data point: the entire global budget of the movement working to reduce animal consumption and animal suffering is less than one fourth of the marketing budget of Restaurant Brands International, the parent company behind fast food chains such as Burger King and Popeyes.

Add to this the lobbying of food producers (and stakeholders in adjacent sectors) who influence regulations, taxes, subsidies and even publicly funded promotion. All of this contributes to the food environment, in which people believe they are choosing freely what to buy.

And yet the food freedom fighter’s irritation is reserved for those pushy, preachy vegans. (For additional insight into why this is so, you can read my article When doing something good makes other people hate you.)

There’s more. Our bodies crave high-calorie foods - especially fatty and sugary ones. In times when food was scarce and survival uncertain, seeking energy-rich foods gave us an advantage. Today, this instinct works against us. Companies exploit it, making their foods as tasty and addictive as possible - just like Facebook and TikTok do everything possible to hijack our attention, in order to boost their bottom line.

Changing the food environment

Rather than trying to motivate individuals with various arguments, we can work on the supply side and try to convince companies or governments to take action. If people don’t on their own tend to make compassionate, sustainable, healthy food choices, and if our food environment is not supporting those options, we need to change that food environment so it becomes more conducive to positive change. We can try to convince the food freedom fighters - and the decision makers - of what I wrote above: that consumers are quite defenseless against market forces that exploit their weaknesses. Rather than opposing restrictions to our “freedom,” we should welcome all the help we can get.

Of course many food freedom fighters will be equally opposed to this approach. Perhaps even more than activists and do-gooders, governments and institutions should stay the hell out of people’s plates. And governments are indeed wary of interfering, not because the evidence is unclear, but because liberty-triggering backlash is predictable. To avoid a sausage-wielding populist running away with half the electorate, politicians prefer to leave things to the consumer. And this consumer says thank you, yes, I’ll decide for myself what I’ll eat, and then proceeds to buy exactly what various forces are pushing him to buy.

One option is to take an even subtler approach, so the public doesn’t realize something is being taken away from them. Institutions can nudge customers by promoting certain options, changing defaults (making the good thing the easy thing), or adjusting prices (but the food freedom fighters better not find out). So much of the real work lies in shaping the environment in which choices are made: making plant-based options more available, more affordable, more normal, and harder to avoid - so that people can keep their sense of freedom while the default direction of society quietly shifts.

The most free

If you’re vegetarian or vegan, you’ve heard it many times: “Are you allowed to eat that?” The question implies that we’re not free to do what we want, and have to follow certain rules. There are rules, of course - sometimes too strictly interpreted or enforced by the vegan community - but basically we follow them because we want to follow them.

Most vegans engage with food far more consciously than the average consumer. They’re more aware of where their food comes from and what’s in it. They’ve set clear criteria for what they will and won’t eat. They seem far less susceptible to advertising. Rather than simply repeating what their parents and grandparents ate, they’ve actively thought about their diet.

So when it comes to their food choices, even if it may not look like it, perhaps no one is as free as vegans.

Here then, is the irony: the food freedom fighters are not defending freedom from vegans - they are defending freedom from the one influence that challenges the status quo.

item.title: Can you eat animals mindfully?
item.description: On Sam Harris, compassion, and the beings we leave out
item.content:encoded:
I’m half-heartedly participating in Real Attention, a 14-day challenge on Sam Harris‘ mindfulness app Waking Up. I can recommend both the app and Sam Harris’ podcast and books. But today’s attention challenge irked me.

Here is the text I found in my inbox:

You eat every day, often while doing something else (…) In these cases, the food is mostly fuel: You appreciate little of its flavor, and even less of its history:
That food came from something—seed, rain, sunshine; and from somewhere—the soil of places you’ve never been; and from someones—the energy and effort of people you’ll never meet.
When you consider this, you realize how much had to happen for just one small piece of food to arrive on your plate. And that inspires gratitude.
The Challenge: Choose one small item of food—a strawberry, a piece of chocolate, a slice of bread. Look at it carefully. Note its color, shape, texture, light, and shadow. Then imagine you can see beyond its appearance and into its history. Picture the dirt, the crops, the hands that harvested them. Then eat slowly.

Animal foods are inconvenient to be mindful about

Animals are conspicuously absent from this exercise. That is not accidental.

When people talk about food and list their favorite recipes, most will think of animal products: a steak, a trout, a cheese platter… But when we’re invited to focus mindfully on our food’s “history”, examples suddenly become plant-based. Strawberries are convenient, lamb chops are not.

Doing this exercise honestly with the foods central to most people’s plates would require imagining slaughter (sometimes without proper stunning) - and the awful, bloody places where this violence occurs. It would require thinking about life-long confinement, mutilations like castration, debeaking or dehorning, about bodies bred for productivity rather than health, about chronic pain, fear, and distress.

These are not marginal issues. They describe the standard reality of animal agriculture. Those who believe none of this applies to the meat they eat are either deceiving themselves or belong to verrrry small minority who only consume wild animals - and even there, “mindfulness” would mean confronting the terror we inflict on them.

People, always just people

Animals are the biggest stakeholders in our food system. We kill and eat hundreds of billions of them every year. Yet even in a mindful eating-exercise, they disappear from view. The attention challenge speaks of “someones,” but then clarifies that this is just about “people you’ll never meet”. Later, it urges us to “soften the boundaries between ourselves and the people who brought us our food.”

What makes this omission worse is that the context here is spirituality - and compassion, which Sam Harris frequently says is central to mindfulness. Yet once again, compassion stops at the species barrier.

The result is sort of perverse: an exercise meant to cultivate awareness and ethical sensitivity ends up encouraging selective attention. Arguably, what matters most here is precisely what remains unexamined. Being grateful for one’s food while systematically omitting the primary victims feels less like mindfulness and more like moral laundering. At the very least, it is a highly selective form of awareness.

One charitable interpretation is that animals are omitted from the exercise in order not to further normalize their consumption. But given that - as in almost any demographic - the majority of Waking Up-users eats animal products, this omission has the opposite effect: it allows participants to remain unexamined. A more honest, and genuinely mindful, version of the challenge might therefore include a sentence like this:

If you are thinking of an animal product, consider honestly what the animal went through. Then decide for yourself whether you are comfortable with that.

All beings

The pattern of forgetting animals can be found in much of spirituality beyond food. When I listen to conversations, meditations, or talks on mindfulness (on the Waking Up app and elsewhere), I find myself noticing who the speakers are referring to.

Almost always, it is people. Rarely is it beings. And yet compassion is relevant to everyone with subjective experiences. On this planet, human animals are only a small fraction of this set. Yet even those who are looking for the highest form of awareness, remain blissfully unaware of the animals in their food.

There are exceptions, of course. French Buddhist monk, author and vegan Matthieu Ricard, thinks refreshingly non-anthropocentric:

“All sentient beings, without exception, strive for happiness but are confused about what can bring them happiness. Because of ignorance, those beings have been wandering in samsara for many, many lifetimes. (...) When I see the state of suffering of those beings and their endless roaming in existence, how can I not harbour an endless feeling of compassion for those beings?
But a mere feeling of compassion is not enough. And today I am powerless to do anything for them. So because of that, I will generate the determination by crossing the door of the spiritual path and practicing it for that ultimate end. I will do so in order to gain the capacity to free all beings from suffering.1

All beings, Sam and team. Please, take non-humans seriously. Help humankind wake up to one of the biggest sources of suffering in this world - inflicted for one of the most trivial of purposes.

item.title: "An Exhibition of Corpses?"
item.description: Making the familiar strange to help people see
item.content:encoded:
Our success in changing individual attitudes and behavior around eating animals remains limited for now, and at this stage I’m more a believer in institutional change. Especially moral messages are hard to swallow for most people, and there’s a lot of resistance to hearing them. Still, this doesn’t stop me and others from searching for effective ways to convey the seriousness of the plight of animals on our planet. Below, I explore one particular approach.

The alien and the butchery

La Belle Verte is a not very well known French film from the nineties. On a distant planet, members of an enlightened society are looking for one among them who will pay a visit to Earth. Familiar with Earth’s reputation as a nasty place, few volunteer - until one brave woman, Mila, steps forward. We follow this humanoid alien through various locations and situations on our planet. In one scene, she bumps into a butcher shop. Looking at the meat in the window, she asks: “What IS this? An exhibition of corpses?”

Then, a customer leaves the shop, and this short conversation ensues:

Mila: “Excuse me ma’am, what is it you just got there?”

Customer: “That’s my meat.”

Mila: “To… do what with?”

Customer (confused): “To eat, of course.”

Mila (with a terrified look on her face): “You are a carnivore?!”

The customer signals to Mila that she’s crazy. But seconds later, because of Mila’s mind-altering powers, she suddenly stops in the street, sits down on the pavement, unwraps the meat, and… stares at it in complete disbelief. For the first time in her life, we assume, this woman wonders about what she’s eating.

In art, the device used in this scene is called defamiliarization or - if you prefer a mysterious Russian-based word - ostranenie. It’s the technique of making the familiar strange, so that the reader or viewer is forced to see ordinary things with fresh eyes. In the case of La Belle Verte, this is done through offering us the perspective of an alien. Mila has no cultural conditioning around meat, no lifelong habituation to the sight of it. She’s not ignorant or naive, but simply unencumbered by the slow normalization that happens when something is everywhere and always.

An outsider’s perspective

Our practice of massively exploiting animals has indeed become so utterly normal that most people never seriously question it. Even I, as an animal activist for thirty years, often have moments where I think: is this really happening? Are we really torturing, killing and eating sentient beings by the billions, every year - all for short-lived gustatory pleasures? All without most people batting an eye? (see my article Gaslit by humanity).

To truly see our world in a new light, an outsider’s perspective is helpful. Since actual outsiders are very hard to find in our global culture, we have to conjure them through imagination. Fiction and thought experiments allow us to inhabit worlds where the current horrors are absent. From that vantage point, through the eyes of our outsiders, we may catch a glimpse of how our reality would look if it were no longer shielded by the veil of normalization.

We can imagine a society and someone standing outside of it - like “the savage” in Huxley’s Brave New World. We can imagine aliens in faraway places, as in La Belle Verte. We can dream up future human beings, who, from a better future look back at us with horrified eyes, as in the 2017 British movie Carnage (see the list at the bottom of this post).

What gives the outsider’s perspective its power is our knowledge or intuition that she’s actually seeing more clearly than we are. A moral relativist would shrug this off: Mila comes from a different culture with different norms, and leave it at that. But for those like me (and you?), who believe there are objectively better and worse ways to act or perceive the world, the outsider’s gaze is - rather than just an interesting thought experiment - a corrective lens, that strips away the distortions of custom and habit.

Make the familiar strange

My guess is that we - even those of us who already care deeply about animals - will only really, deeply realize what is going on here once it’s all over.

I remain convinced that we can make it so. Meat alternives will help. So will books, movies or thought experiments that defamiliarize, and show us that we are currently living in the pre-history of a truly civilized world.

Write them, make them, invent them.

So that some day, everyone will look at a piece of meat like our alien Mila does: with the terrifying clarity of someone seeing a corpse.

And so that everyone will one day wonder:

What the hell were we doing?
