item.title: All your heart and all your head
item.description: On empathy, rationality, and helping animals
item.content:encoded:
Last week I was giving a talk on animal welfare and diet change to a general audience. During the Q&A, a young woman of around twenty said something like the following:

“I consider myself quite an altruistic person, and I choose plant-based options regularly. But somehow, I can’t feel all this empathy that you seem to have for the animals. Sometimes a vegan friend will explain to me everything that happens, and somehow I can’t truly feel it. What do I do in such a case?”

What, indeed, do you do when you want to care but can’t?

In most cases, I’m skeptical when people tell me they don’t care about what happens to animals. Sometimes it’s posturing for others, or a lack of self-examination. Another reason can be that they are not familiar enough with animals, and what they are cognitiviely and emotionally capable of. More importantly, people are protecting themselves against caring, because caring has real-life consequences. If you care about what happens to a pig and want to be honest with yourself, you’ll probably have difficulty eating pig meat, at least from an animal that was factory-farmed. So in order not to have to change your behavior (bothersome!), you’ll try not to care, and you avoid things that would lead to caring more.

Still, I do encounter people who tell me very honestly that they don’t care. Especially when I can see that they would like to care, I take them seriously, as I did in the case of this young woman. Her question made me consider - as I often do - what exactly it is that people need in order to change.

We are often quick to think that that’s empathy or being emotionally moved by something. And we may surmise that this is both a necessary and sufficient condition to change.

Yet clearly, that is not the case.

I tried to answer this young woman as best I could. To start with, I acknowledged her issue and said that we can’t help what we feel, and that sometimes, I don’t feel much for something that other people seem very moved or shaken by. Secondly, I asked if she was sure that she was not touched by animal suffering at all, and suggested maybe she watch a fragment of Earthlings or Dominion (warning her that these are extremely graphic documentaries which I’ve never been able to watch myself). She nodded and wrote down the titles.

Thinking without feeling

Thirdly, I said that it may not be necessary to feel the issue, and be moved by what happens to animals. She could also, in principle, change her views and behavior on the basis of mere information - such as the facts and statistics that I had been providing. One can, I think, conclude on the basis of reason alone that pain and suffering are not good things and we should aspire to reduce them for everyone who experiences them - and at least not to cause more of them. She seemed to agree.

That empathy and care are not sufficient conditions for change can be easily seen. So many people care about something but don’t change their behavior. It’s perhaps a bit harder to see that rationality by itself can lead to good behavior. But one can imagine a robot - who is not conscious - demonstrating perfectly rational and ethical (from a consequentialist perspective) behavior. The robot doesn’t feel any of the suffering, but will try (if it’s programmed the way you and I would program it) to avoid it and reduce it.

People, however, are not robots. We experience so many emotions and desires - which robots don’t suffer from - that pull us in non-optimal and irrational directions. So if a person is not a perfectly or even mostly rational creature, who aligns their values with their beliefs, some extra motivation or drive, in the form of empathy or care, is probably most useful, and even necessary.

There’s this saying: you can lead a horse to water, but you can’t make it drink. A long time ago, at a conference, I heard the late Tom Regan say in a talk: philosophy can lead a mind to water, but only emotion can make it drink. I don’t remember the exact context, but given that Regan is the author of The Case for Animal Rights, a very dense, philosophical book, I assume he meant that these cerebral arguments are not enough, and that emotion or empathy has to be involved somehow.

How much empathy is too much?

No matter whether being emotionally moved by animals or not is necessary, at the very least it’s clear to me that this is a spectrum, and perhaps the question is rather: how much empathy is necessary? Some people may get very emotionally moved by these things, others only slightly. The same goes for rationality: some will attach a lot of importance to objective facts and numbers (and base their choices on them). Others might not, and make sub-optimal decisions because they are too emotional and caring. Therefore another question is: how much empathy is too much?

I often feel this tension in myself. I hardly ever seek it out, but seeing coverage of cruel animal treatment may renew or boost my motivation. It may spur me to write or share or do something that hopefully has some kind of positive impact. On the other hand, the result may also be that I react mostly from my emotions, and say or write things that people who are not in my shoes can’t relate to, and will find alienating - for instance because I’m too aggressive. Or I might suggest people donate to a charity that posted something I was very moved by, while the more rational thing would be to ask them to donate to a highly effective charity.

We can be really blinded by our emotions and our empathy. Caring can turn into frustration and anger, which - while sometimes energizing - are often not productive. Moreover, to be moved (let alone angry or frustrated) all the time may also be detrimental to one’s personal sustainability.

I’m not sure if I can conclude on much else than the cliché that we need both emotion/empathy and rationality - the former can help spur us into action, the latter can help select which actions are the most fruitful.

The combination is what’s most beautiful: an analytical person who is crying, or a very emotional person who is doing her best to sort out what is the best thing to do: both of these cases… move me very much.

Thank you for caring and thinking, with all your heart and all your head.

item.title: Should farmed animals have a labour union?
item.description: An interview with Marjolein De Rooij
item.content:encoded:
Look at any illustration of our food system. You’ll see a lot of parties represented there. Yet the biggest stakeholders, the animals, are always absent. They have no place at the table - but are served on the table, for another big “steakholder”: the consumer.

Could we help animals, thought Dutch activist Marjolein De Rooij, and protect them against exploitation and unfair treatment by giving them labour rights? The idea gave birth to an non-profit called the Animal Labour Union, which offers a refreshing way to look at the situation of farmed animals. At the same time, this framing raises some obvious questions among those who - like myself - prefer to see the farmed animal industry gone entirely. I recently attended the Union’s conference and spoke with Marjolein about her initiative.

Marjolein, what exactly is the Animal Labour Union and what do you want to achieve?

The core idea behind the labour union is that we approach animals differently. I’m specifically talking about working animals—animals who are part of an economic system, which means there’s a financial component and an employer-employee relationship involved. These factors determine how these animals are treated. I focus on working animals in animal agriculture because the numbers are highest there, but this could extend to police dogs, guide dogs, animals in research, entertainment, sports, and more.

We were inspired by human labour unions. About 150 years ago, most employees were uneducated, had little power, and came from lower social classes. Many were exploited by their employers. They weren’t taken seriously and needed representatives to help them—not because they couldn’t speak, but because they weren’t heard. That is the situation of working animals today. We want to see them not only as victims, but as active participants in the labour process. Unfortunately, I couldn’t legally set up an association where the members are animals—they are not legal persons—so we set up a foundation and have donors.

Hasn’t the situation for animals improved? Employers don’t have complete power over their working animals. They’re constrained by animal welfare regulations.

Often, animal welfare laws can be ignored if the employer finds them too expensive to implement. Society agrees that cutting off a pig’s tail is wrong, yet it’s still allowed because farmers claim it’s impossible to stop. Human labour law works differently—there’s no room for such negotiation. A construction worker must wear a helmet, even if the employer considers helmets too costly.

Seeing farmed animals as employees is clearly better than seeing them as property. But since there’s no payment, contract, or mutual agreement, isn’t it more accurate to call them slaves?

It is indeed slavery, or forced labour, and I’m aware the parallel with human workers breaks down in several places. A human worker’s career ends with paid retirement, while animals die at the end of their working life—which may be short. An animal never chose this. From birth, animals must do what they are forced to do. The problem is that when you call farmed animals slaves, you are calling farmers slaveholders, and this will kill any chance of dialogue.

Framing farmed animals as working animals opens new possibilities and perspectives. For instance, in the Netherlands, it’s forbidden to compete on labour standards. Someone who fills shelves in a supermarket will earn the same at another supermarket. But the same retailers are allowed to compete on the working conditions of the animals whose body parts or products they sell. Drawing these kinds of parallels makes the animals a subject of conversation. They get agency and empowerment.

Abolitionist activists might argue that the “worker” frame risks cementing the system by creating a situation that feels “good enough.”

I am vegan myself and support abolishing the use of animals for food, but this will be a slow, long process. We need to pursue many paths to reach our goal. Labor law is dynamic, not static. 150 years ago, we started with a half-Sunday off and one week of unpaid leave per year. Today, we are discussing parental leave and the right to work from home. Labor law evolves with what society finds acceptable. I believe giving animals a voice could lead to abolition. A cow might say: “You can have some milk, but first I need to feed my calf. I also choose who fathers my calves, and I need a comfortable place to rest.” Very few forms of animal husbandry could ever meet such standards, though some might work with a consent model. In any case, I don’t think a labour law approach will increase acceptance of the industry.

Can you tell us about the six labour rights you advocate for?

First is the right to a safe working environment. For instance, barns must be protected from fire. Hundreds of thousands of animals die in barn fires every year because we don’t take security seriously enough. The same applies to low-emission flooring systems—cows may crash through the floor and die in the manure pit.

The second is the right to a healthy working environment. So far, the industry has focused mainly on physical health: disease, pain, and injury. But we also need to consider mental health. Boredom, for instance, could be a serious problem, yet we don’t address it until it causes physical issues like chickens pecking at each other or cannibalism.

Third is the right to a social life. Unlike human workers, farmed animals live where they work. They should have more freedom to choose their companions and live in intergenerational groups—for instance, cows with their calves. We must adapt the systems to the animals’ needs, not the other way around.

Then there’s the right to rest, vacation, and retirement. People often joke about this, but it’s perfectly possible to take it seriously. For example, we can choose not to inseminate an animal immediately after giving birth and give them more time to recover.

Retirement seems more difficult to arrange?

Yes, after their working life, humans live until they die. For many animals, the end of their “career” is also their death, since their bodies are eaten. But dairy cows, for instance, could be kept for at least a year after their last calf. We could extend their lifespan by spreading production—the same milk over six years instead of four. If animals live longer, you need fewer of them. Of course, not all those millions of animals—consider the chickens!—can get an actual retirement, but even a symbolic right would be meaningful.

The fifth right is freedom from violence. I realize that killing animals is violent, so we could never fully implement this right. But I don’t just mean human violence—I also mean violence between animals caused by their living conditions. For example, facilities that breed parent stock for egg-laying hens keep hens and roosters together in crowded spaces, and many hens get injured.

Finally, there is the right to have a say—to be represented. Certain human parties need to voice the animals’ concerns to the industry, but this is happening only to a very limited extent. For instance, in a Dutch commission on humane animal husbandry, there are 17 stakeholders from the industry and only one animal protection group.

You’re doing research into animal language, including AI. Do you think we’ll ever understand animals, so that they can better represent themselves?

Animals communicate with us constantly—in a sense, animal protest happens every day. Yet we often fail to listen. AI could be a crucial tool here, as it excels at distinguishing vocal patterns and subtle sounds that escape the human ear. In crowded agricultural environments, it’s nearly impossible for humans to isolate, for instance, “pleasure calls” from the background noise.

Farmers often argue that if an animal wasn’t doing well, it wouldn’t be productive.

That reasoning is flawed. 70% of hens have breastbone fractures, yet they still lay eggs despite the pain. 25% of cows have udder infections or are lame, but they continue producing milk. I think it’s crucial that farmers are not the sole judges of their animals’ living conditions. Imagine if Schiphol Airport claimed KLM takes care of its baggage handlers well enough and there should be no interference or unions. We don’t accept that argument in any human workplace. Farmers need to make many financial decisions, and when money is tight, animal welfare is often the first to be sacrificed.

What about the argument that farmers know their animals best?

I’d say most suffer from professional blindness. A farmer with 200 cows or 300 sows doesn’t have time to check each animal individually. Instead, they rely on totals and averages, tracked through technology. Their phone alerts them to a drop in production, but they may not notice a cow with a sore hind leg. Many modern farmers have lost traditional knowledge about keeping animals alive without industrial systems. Research shows many can’t even recognize the sound of a cow calling for her calf. Farmers also have an incentive not to bond with animals that leave every week—it hurts too much. Research shows that talking gently to pigs reduces their stress by 25%, yet almost all farmers say they don’t talk to them.

Are you happy with what you’ve done so far with the Animal Labour Union?

To be honest, I don’t think one animal is better off today than four years ago because of us. But we’ve started a movement, and we’ve been heard. I’m on the radio every two weeks, in major newspapers, and was selected number one in the Dutch “Sustainable Top 100.” We received funding from the Ministry of Agriculture, and they invite me to give lectures and workshops. Various stakeholders find the six rights we champion to be a useful framework that highlights many areas for improvement.

What are your priorities for the future?

I’m very concerned about technological innovation. Governments invest in “sustainable” livestock farming to solve climate problems, but ignore the interests of the individual animals. Air scrubbers can make barn fires spread faster. Measures to reduce ammonia emissions may make the barn climate less healthy for animals. In Denmark, supplements to make cows emit less methane caused animals to suddenly die. If we adapt a cow’s digestive system, who says they don’t have continuous stomach pain?

I’m also very interested in what makes animals happy. There is a lot of focus on reducing pain and suffering - they negatively impact production - there is little commercial incentive to study animal happiness. I think that even in terrible circumstances, humans and non-humans can still experience moments of happiness. As long as the animals are in the systems, can we, apart from reducing their pain, perhaps also look at how we can increase their happiness? Some would warn here against anthropomorphism - ascribing human characteristics to animals. But I agree with primatologist Frans de Waal, who said denying animals certain characteristics that they do have - anthropodenial - causes more suffering than we think. So always and everywhere, when we make decisions that affect animals, we should wonder: how does the cow, the pig, the chicken… think about this?

item.title: Realism or optimism: what helps animals more?
item.description: Last weekend I attended and spoke at the Vegan and Animal Rights Conference (VARC) in Manchester, alongside four hundred like-minded people.
item.content:encoded:
Last weekend I attended and spoke at the Vegan and Animal Rights Conference (VARC) in Manchester, alongside four hundred like-minded people. We did the usual networking, strategizing, learning, and karaoke singing, and like many others I left inspired, connected, and energized (thank you, VARC team!) Some volunteers were walking around collecting data from attendees, which would hopefully show funders that the conference is an effective use of their money. I’m all for measurement, but with some things the value seems so obvious that it may not require overanalysis.

There were many great talks and speakers, but I want to focus here on two sessions, which described the same movement in very different moods. They made me consider, once again, what we can realistically achieve.

Connor’s radical realism

In his talk A journey of a thousand steps, Connor Jackson from Anima UK spoke from the trenches of corporate welfare campaigning. Connor has spent over a decade leading Anima’s UK work, combining undercover investigations with corporate pressure and activist mobilization, and building a track record of pushing major food businesses to improve chicken welfare standards.

Connor is vegan and wants to see an end to animal exploitation, but he has his reasons for campaigning for better living conditions for layer hens and slower-growing broilers. After decades of activism, he said, the number of farmed animals continues to increase. And chickens, of course, represent the vast majority of farmed animals. Connor believes the movement is “overwhelmingly failing” these creatures and needs to change its approach.

He thinks cage-free campaigns may be the most successful campaigns in animal rights history, giving hundreds of millions of birds a better, though far from ideal, life. Activists who can’t see a difference between caged and cage-free, or between fast- and slower-growing breeds of chickens, are not taking animal suffering seriously enough. Being able to spread your wings, escaping the pain of walking on metal grates for over a year, access to sunlight, the ability to escape aggressive flockmates… are all very meaningful for the birds.

Connor knows that cage-free systems are not the end point, but the strategy is to progress in steps: from battery cages, to cage-free, then to free range, to organic and beyond. With such incremental reforms, we can progressively undo the focus on efficiency that harms animals, raise their political status, and shift what society deems acceptable.

This will take time. Although he calls himself an optimist, Connor believes many activists’ dreams and goals - such as ending animal exploitation within the next few decades - are misguided, and that we’ll be stuck with intensive animal agriculture for many decades to come.

Harley’s optimism

In his talk The sleeping giant: unleashing the power of the animal movement, Harley Brewer, an activist with Just Stop Oil, Extinction Rebellion, and Animal Rising, offered a different story.** While many media outlets are keen to report that veganism is collapsing, Harley argues that the data do not match that narrative, and that the number of vegans has grown dramatically over the past decades. He believes that, as a movement, we think we are smaller than we are: in the UK, there are not just 3% vegans, 6% vegetarians, and 5% pescatarians, but also 25% flexitarians. Together, Harley says, that’s 39% of the public taking part in an economic boycott by actively reducing meat consumption. All these people are taking active steps to help put an end to factory farming.

If any other movement had 40% of the public taking part, Harley argued, it would not see itself as failing. We can absolutely win this and there is no reason we couldn’t end factory farming in our lifetime. Harley pointed to several recent victories: universities going partially or even fully plant-based, Proveg UK swapping nearly 60 million meals in UK schools to plant-based ones, and the Communities Against Factory Farming delaying or stopping every single factory farm application.*

Winning will require thinking politically (the government is the ultimate decision-maker), building coalitions across ideologies, and transforming the people who participate. Veganism should not be a prerequisite for joining the movement - the only requirements are a willingness to work on the issue and an ability to collaborate. Most of all, according to Harley, we need to believe that we can win.

Winning without wishful thinking

I’m not sure who I agree with more: Connor Jackson or Harley Brewer. It’s not obvious, in part because they’re using focusing on different things and using different metrics.

I do believe Connor is right that making a difference in the lives of hundreds of millions, and eventually billions, of chickens is significant. And I also think Harley is right that, despite the horrible and loud voices wishing vegans and the animal rights movement to hell, we have more support than we think we have.

But aside from asking which of these narratives is most factual - a question we’re not going to resolve here - we can also ask which one is most helpful.

Some will say that what’s most helpful is what’s most factual. That’s a reasonable view. If you believe you can do less than you actually can, you might aim lower than you should. Conversely, if you believe you have superpowers, you might set unrealistic goals and end up disappointed and frustrated. It seems, therefore, quite important to have a clear sense of what we can realistically achieve.

And yet at the same time, I also believe in self-fulfilling prophecies: believing you can do more than you think may energize you to actually do it. In that sense, as Karl Popper said, optimism is a moral duty.

I’m not sure whether realism or optimism will get us the furthest. We probably need a combination: optimistic realism or realistic optimism. And what’s most useful may often vary individually, on the person and where they are, psychologicially. If you feel burned out or dejected, a dose of Harley would do you good. If you’re overly optimistic, believing everything will sort itself out quickly, take a dose of Connor.

Because one thing seems clear: we will have to keep working as hard as we can. Lewis Bollard of Coefficient Giving put it aptly: the end of factory farming is neither inevitable nor impossible.

It won’t be easy, but it can be done.

We should dream big and appreciate small steps, put in the work and think creatively, do our research and find out the best interventions and tactics, and collaborate with everyone who thinks factory farming is a disaster (no matter what they eat).

item.title: Prisoners of compassion
item.description: The woman across from me and my girlfriend says she’s exhausted.
item.content:encoded:
The woman across from me and my girlfriend says she’s exhausted.

She’s an old friend, and we’re meeting her over lunch. Let me call her Annie (not her real name). Annie has been running an animal sanctuary in France for many years.

She’s 69, and apart from the occasional help of volunteers, does it all by herself. She’s in my country, Belgium, for a brief visit. In fact, all her visits are brief, because she can’t leave her 120 animals - horses, donkeys, goats, cats, dogs, chickens, and more - alone for long. Even during these few days away, a volunteer told her over the phone that a donkey needed to be euthanized after a freak accident. “Why,” Annie said with a sigh, “do these things continue to happen?”

Annie would like to move back to Belgium, where she’s originally from. She feels very lonely in the south of France, where few people understand her. She’s surrounded by locals who eat the animals she would save, hunters who shoot them, and vets who don’t get why she cares so much.

Annie spends all her time and money on her animals, whom she saved from abandonment, neglect, or slaughter. People know how to find her. They often emotionally blackmail her, saying that if she doesn’t take a particular animal, it will be euthanized or slaughtered. Annie has a very hard time saying no in these situations.

Sitting across from her, it’s hard not to feel that her life is no longer entirely her own. That something else is making the decisions.

We could call Annie a prisoner of compassion.* She’s less free than many people are because of how much she cares. Her compassion decides when she travels, how long she stays, how she spends her money, and how much rest she allows herself. While many caring people may feel like this to some extent, it may be worse for frontline animal helpers in animal sanctuaries or shelters.

We have our own sanctuary (Feathery Forest). It’s entirely my girlfriend Melanie’s project. She loves to do hands-on work with animals, while I’m more of a cerebral person who prefers the top-down work. Sanctuaries, and people who take care of individual animals, can only help a small number of animals directly. Costs are high, and animals require a lot of space. For that reason, among activists who focus on impact and effectiveness, sanctuaries sometimes have a difficult reputation: resources could be better spent to help larger numbers of animals.

I think there’s truth to this criticism, but sitting across Annie - and living at a sanctuary myself - I can hardly allow myself to think it. The thing is, I am so glad sanctuaries and shelters are there for the animals, who will remain the victims of human indifference and cruelty for as long as these traits exist in us.

The frontline helpers are the ones who get up close and personal with the misery and the surplus of animals. They incur costs. They experience the heartbreak of having to say no. They face physical and mental exhaustion. They see their animals die, one after another, at a pace that doesn’t even give them time to mourn. They absorb a part of the world’s cruelty so that others don’t have to see it directly. They are the ones, it seems, whom compassion is holding most tightly in its grip.

Looking at Annie, I was thinking about something that could help her. I’m guilty of increasing people like Annie’s burden: when I encounter an animal in need, I’ll find a shelter or sanctuary, or someone who’s got too many animals to take care of already. That’s because I don’t know myself what to do with the animal - certainly not if it’s in need of medical care. At the very least, I leave a donation.

I told Annie something I hope could bring some comfort: that a quick, painless death - euthanasia - is not the worst thing in the world. And that on a planet where there are more animals in need than there are people, resources, or space to care for them, tragic trade-offs are unavoidable. Refusing to accept that can mean pushing people like her past their limits.

When we said goodbye, Annie would soon return to her animals in France. Back to the same responsibilities and the same impossible choices.

I hope that she, and all other prisoners of compassion, don’t just appreciate what holds them hostage, but can also take pride in it. Even if compassion limits their freedom, it is also the reason so many animals are safe. Most of all, their work is an inspiration. In a world where animal exploitation is legal, subsidized and everywhere, they are the ones who remind us of all that humans can be.

* I came across this term in the writing of the Dutch author Charlotte Mutsaers

item.title: Why I've made peace with shiitake-infused beef burgers (for now)
item.description: Insights from the Plant FWD conference 2026
item.content:encoded:
Plant FWD - a major alt-protein conference held annually in the Netherlands - almost did not happen this year.

The founders increasingly struggled to make the event financially viable. After announcing there would be no more editions, they found a buyer: a company that owns conference venues. As a result, this year it moved from Amsterdam to rural Barneveld - which apparently is the chicken capital of the world.

All of this is to say something we all already know: the climate around alt protein has shifted a lot lately. Maybe seven years ago, there was a sense that the revolution was imminent, that plant-based meat was ready to take off, following the smartphone’s trajectory, and that cultivated meat would land on supermarket shelves within a decade.

But the bubble burst, and we ended up disappointed. According to one analysis, most consumers started trying vegan burgers, nuggets, and sausages for health reasons. Then inflation hit, and at the same time the narrative spread that these products were ultra-processed and not healthier than meat. Consumers saw no reason to keep buying products that offered no clear health benefits, cost more, and tasted worse. Today, the crazy money that poured into alt food companies back then seems largely to have dried up.

Being less optimistic, however, does not mean we are dead. Quite the contrary. The vibe at the conference was great, and in the closing session most attendees said they left more optimistic than they arrived.

The age of the hybrids

One of the reasons to be hopeful - and a topic of focus throughout the conference - is that hybrid meat seems to be doing well. It’s now also known as balanced meat: products like sausages, burgers or minced meat that are partly animal, partly something else (plant-based, fungi, or - hopefully soon - cultivated).

Hybrid products were in the talks and breakout sessions, and were offered as snacks to try (I didn’t). If - like me - you want to see an end to animal food production, you may be skeptical of these mixed products. They are at least half animal-based, so they still cause a lot of animal suffering. And what if they delay - possibly forever - the end goal by offering a moral loophole: a way for consumers to feel they are part of the change while still participating in the harm?

Here, however, are some reasons why I think (without being sure) that the animal movement should welcome the growth of hybrid meat:

  1. These products reduce a lot of suffering, and right now have more potential to do so than vegan products. Look at this simple slide I made for a presentation. Suppose only 5% of a fast-food chain’s hamburger sales are vegan burgers (left). Now compare that to all their burgers being 25% plant-based (right). In reality, just 2% of Burger King US’s burgers sold are the vegan Impossible Burgers.

  1. If hybrid is a winning category, it can help strengthen the economic viability of the alt protein sector, since many companies might produce both plant-based products and plant-based ingredients for hybrid products.

  2. Success for the hybrid category should mean reduced meat sales, which may negatively impact the traditional meat industry.

  3. I can imagine that getting used to hybrid products could shift people’s thinking. Meat might start to feel less like an all-or-nothing category, and the idea of plant-based meat could start to feel more normal.

Going for umami

Michael Fox (middle initial actually J) from the Australian company Fable laid out a concrete case for hybrid products. As an ethical vegan, Fox started by creating a pulled shiitake mushroom product, but now focuses on developing minced shiitake ingredients to blend with minced beef.

The benefits of shiitake and other fungi are impressive. They’re exceptionally nutrient-dense and a great source of fiber (which meat lacks), vitamin D, iron, and protein. Fungi are closer to animal products than plants are, so they require less processing than, for example, legumes when they are turned into meat-like products. Shiitake are also excellent for boosting the umami taste, especially when combined with beef. In blind tastings, shiitake-beef products consistently win out over pure beef products and are often described as “more meaty” than meat, even when they contain 50% mushrooms. They can also be 20% cheaper.

The first successes for Fable are in. After very well-received trials, Compass Group, the world’s largest food service company, is working to replace 30% of its minced beef with a 50/50 blend, aiming to eventually reach 90%. JBS, the world’s largest meat company, launched a shiitake-infused burger in one of its brands in Australia.

Fox ended with some advice: alt protein companies must set the bar really high before launching products: inferior ones hurt the category and erode consumer trust. If your product doesn’t taste better than meat, Fox said, if it isn’t cheaper and healthier than meat, and if consumers don’t perceive it as better than meat, don’t launch it.

Mycelium: going the way of the leafcutter ants

Another fungi enthusiast on stage was Paul Shapiro, CEO of The Better Meat Co, which grows mycelium, a fibrous, meat-like structure in close to its natural state. He explained that leafcutter ants have actually domesticated mycelium since many millions of years, long before human agriculture.

Shapiro framed fungi fermentation as an antidote to the problems that have plagued the alternative meat sector. It requires little processing, and turning low-value carbohydrates into high-value protein, from inoculation to harvest, takes just 17 hours (compared with 6 weeks for chickens, 5 months for pigs, and over a year for cows).

The good news is also that there are thousands of species of mycelium, each with different flavors, textures, nutritional profiles, colors, and smells. At the moment, Quorn, the OG of mycelium, uses just one species and is responsible for 99% of all mycoprotein sold. There is, in other words, still a whole world to explore.

In terms of impact: for seven years now, the Better Meat Co has been selling to Perdue Farms, which the poultry company uses in their Chicken Plus range (50% chicken, 50% plant-based). Shapiro estimates that this deal alone has resulted in approximately 600,000 fewer chickens being raised and slaughtered.

Good inventions, not good intentions

Paul Shapiro was an animal activist long before he became an entrepreneur (I remember doing protests with him in front of fur stores, over 25 years ago). After years of grassroots activism and congressional lobbying, he became a firm believer that technological innovation, rather than moral advocacy, will help wean the masses off animal-based meat. He points to inventions like fountain pens, cars, and kerosene, which replaced quill pens, horse-drawn carriages, and whale oil lamps, respectively, and spared countless animals.

For animal advocates, such pragmatism may feel both like a relief and a bit of an insult at the same time. A relief because it suggests a path that does not depend on mass moral awakening. And an insult because it reminds us of how limited moral persuasion can be. Indeed, we do wish the world would change through an endless series of individual conversions: the meat-eater sees the truth, feels the horror, becomes compassionate and joins Team Vegan.

But this approach fails more often than it succeeds. So we need products people can consume without changing their habits or even their values. It’s a less satisfying story, because it doesn’t flatter our sense of being right, and it does not reward the part of us that wants the public to finally “get it.” But perhaps it’s the story that moves the most animals out of the system in the shortest time.

Technological innovations do not render moral advocacy useless. They make it more likely to succeed. Once we’ve made ourselves less dependent on animal products, through plant-based, cultivated, or hybrid alternatives, we may finally be free to see meat and dairy, and our treatment of animals, for what they are.
